questions.q: Two generals on separate hills must coordinate a joint attack via messengers who might be captured. No messenger's delivery can ever be confirmed with total certainty. Using any finite number of confirmation messages sent back and forth, can the two generals ever be guaranteed to reach common knowledge of the attack time?
choices: Yes, but only if they use a trusted third-party messenger
Yes, but only if the message length is long enough to include a checksum
No — no finite number of messages can ever guarantee both generals have common knowledge of the attack time
Yes, as long as they exchange at least 3 confirmation messages

questions.q: For any ranked-choice voting system with 3 or more candidates, is it possible to design one that always satisfies all three of: no single dictator, respects unanimous voter preference, and is unaffected by irrelevant candidates being added or removed?
choices: Yes, but only when there are exactly 3 candidates
No — Arrow's Impossibility Theorem proves no such ranked voting system can satisfy all three simultaneously
Yes, ranked-pairs voting satisfies all three
Yes, instant-runoff voting satisfies all three

questions.q: In a road network where every driver selfishly picks their fastest available route, a new road is added connecting two existing junctions, giving everyone an additional route option. According to Braess's paradox, what can happen to the average travel time for everyone at the new equilibrium?
choices: It stays exactly the same, since equilibrium travel time is fixed by total traffic volume alone
It only affects drivers who choose to use the new road
It can get worse for every driver, even though everyone now has strictly more route choices
It always gets better or stays the same, since more options can never hurt

questions.q: Gabriel's Horn is formed by rotating the curve y = 1/x for x ≥ 1 around the x-axis. It has a finite volume (π cubic units) when computed by integration. What is its total surface area?
choices: Exactly π, same as the volume
Finite, and larger than the volume
Zero, since the horn narrows to an infinitely thin point
Infinite — the surface area diverges even though the volume is finite
